chunks: And what al-Hasan ibn Mahbub narrated from Hanan ibn Sadir from Sadir, who said:
Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) said: My father used to make up (qada') the daytime nawafil at night while traveling, and he would not complete the obligatory prayer [in full].

Regarding these two reports, [the interpretation lies in] one of two things: one of them is that it should be understood as [indicating the] lifting of hardship (haraj) for one who prays at night what he missed during the day, even if that is not recommended (mustahabb). This is indicated by...

key_terms.رَفْعِ الْحَرَجِ: raf' al-haraj — the lifting/removal of hardship; a recognized principle of Islamic jurisprudence invoked to explain permissive (not prescriptive) rulings
key_terms.مُسْتَحَبًّا: mustahabb — a recommended act; rewarded if done, but not sinful to omit
key_terms.نَوَافِلَ: nawafil — supererogatory prayers that are praiseworthy but not obligatory
key_terms.يَقْضِي: yaqdi — to perform qada', i.e., to make up a prayer missed at its proper time

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on making up daytime supererogatory prayers (nawafil) at night during travel in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) reports that his father, Imam al-Baqir (AS), would perform qada' of the daytime nawafil at night during travel, while shortening the obligatory prayers as required of a traveler. This is the fourth hadith in al-Istibsar's chapter on daytime nawafil during travel; Shaykh al-Tusi appends juristic commentary offering that these two seemingly permissive reports should be reconciled as indicating mere removal of hardship (rafa' al-haraj), not as establishing a recommended (mustahabb) practice.
